segments.say: Now let the rainy street fade gently into the distance, and let's travel somewhere else. Take a slow breath in, and a slower breath out. In your mind, you're standing at the foot of a long, green hillside, just as the afternoon is ending. The air is mild and still. Somewhere above you, a narrow path winds upward between rows of vines, and there's no hurry at all to climb it.

The vines grow in long, tidy rows, following the curve of the hill like lines of handwriting. It's early autumn here too, and the leaves are turning, some still green, some butter yellow, a few already the color of old copper. Between the rows, the grass is soft and cool. You walk slowly, one hand trailing along the leaves, feeling how smooth and cool they are against your fingertips.

Hanging beneath the leaves, there are clusters of dark grapes, round and heavy, with a pale dusty bloom on their skins. The harvest is nearly done, and the last bunches wait patiently for their turn. They've spent all summer simply growing, drinking the sun and the rain, asking nothing of anyone. There's something restful in that. Some of the best things in the world are made just by time, and warmth, and being left alone.

The hill has all the time in the world. Every vine on it has grown slowly, year after year, adding a little each season. No single day made them strong, and no single day needed to. Tonight you can borrow some of that patience. Let your own pace be as slow as the hillside's, and let whatever you're carrying be carried one gentle step at a time.

show.text: The hill has all the time in the world.

segments.say: When you reach a gentle bend in the path, you stop and turn around. The whole hillside lies spread out below you. The rows of vines glow in the last light, gold and copper, with long soft shadows between them. Beyond them, a faint mist is gathering in the valley, thin and silvery. The sky above is turning from peach to rose to a deep, quiet blue, and the first star is just beginning to show.

The sun sinks lower, slowly, like someone setting down a heavy bag. The light turns honey-colored, then amber, then a very soft rose. It warms your face for a moment longer, and you close your eyes and let it. The warmth lingers on your cheeks, your forehead, the backs of your hands. Then, little by little, it fades, and the cool evening air takes its place, fresh and calm.

Let's gather what's around you here. Long rows of vines, curving over the hill. Leaves of copper and gold. Ripe, dark grapes, hanging in the shade. A thin mist, settling in the valley. And the very first star, glimmering above the ridge. Take them all in with one slow breath. There's nothing to do on this hillside except be here, and be quiet, while the evening comes.

Beside the path, there's a low stone wall, built long ago from pale, rough stones. You sit down on it, and it's still warm from the day's sun. The warmth seeps through your clothes and into your back. You rest your hands on your knees. Little lichens, orange and gray, dot the stones around you, growing a tiny bit each year, in no hurry, and perfectly content.

The air at dusk carries all kinds of gentle smells. Warm earth, and crushed leaves, and the faint sweetness of ripe fruit. Somewhere there's woodsmoke, drifting from a farmhouse chimney far below. Breathe it in slowly, all the way down, and let it out again. Each breath is cool and sweet, and each one carries away a little more of the day's tiredness, until your chest feels wide and soft.

Evening asks very little of us. It doesn't ask us to be productive, or clever, or even awake. It only asks us to slow down as the light slows down, and to let the day finish without us. Everything on this hillside is doing exactly that. The leaves are letting go of the light, the grapes are letting go of the sun, and you can let go of whatever is left of today.

show.text: Evening asks very little of us.

segments.say: Down at the bottom of the hill, a small farmhouse with a red-tiled roof is switching on its lights, one window at a time. They glow yellow and friendly against the darkening slope. Someone is cooking supper down there, perhaps, or setting a table, or simply sitting with a book. It looks like a place where nobody is ever rushed, and where a late evening is always welcome.

Some things are made by waiting. A vineyard knows this better than anyone. It can't be hurried, and it can't be forced, only tended gently and given time. Rest works the same way. You don't make yourself fall asleep. You simply make the conditions kind, and then you wait, and sleep arrives by itself, like dusk arriving on the hill.

show.text: Some things are made by waiting.

segments.say: The blue of the sky deepens, and the stars begin to appear, one at a time. First one, then three, then more than you could count. They sparkle softly above the dark curve of the hill. The vines have turned into quiet silhouettes now, long, soft lines against the last pale glow in the west. And the night, wide and unhurried, settles in all around you.

You lie back on the cool, soft grass at the edge of the path, and look up. The sky is enormous. Your arms rest loosely at your sides, and the ground holds you up without any effort on your part. Your breathing has slowed all by itself. In, and out. In, and out. You feel small in the very best way, safe and unimportant and held.

As the stars glimmer, let go of a few more things. Your shoulders, which can sink a little lower. Your hands, which can open a little wider. Your breath, which can slow a little more. And your thoughts, which can drift apart like the mist over the valley, thinner and thinner, until there's mostly silver quiet left.

Take a long, slow breath in, and imagine it's the cool, clean air of the hillside. Hold it for a moment, lightly. Then let it flow out into the dark, all the way to the far ridge and beyond. Do that once more, and notice how much quieter you feel inside. The night air has a way of making room. There's space in you now, wide and calm, like the valley below.

The whole hillside is asleep now. The vines rest in their rows, the grapes rest in their leaves, and the stone wall rests in the dark, storing up what's left of the warmth. A soft breeze moves through the leaves, barely there at all. You could stay here as long as you like. There's nothing to leave for, and nobody waiting. Just the stars, and the slow night, and you.

Let yourself drift now, like a leaf drifting down onto the grass. Your eyes are heavy. Your face is soft. Your body feels as though it's sinking into the ground, wrapped in the cool, sweet air of a late autumn night. And somewhere beyond the hill, far away, the next quiet place is already waiting for you, whenever you're ready to go there. There's no need to look for it. It will find you, softly, just as the evening found the hill. Until then, simply rest, and let the stars keep watch over the sleeping vines.
